Maladaptive Strategies.value: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events

Threat.value: I feel on guard even inside my own home
I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations

Memory.value: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.

vignette: Thompson, a 46-year-old South Eastern Asian male and software engineer, had served in combat years ago, an experience that still deeply affected his daily life. He was married and worked in a tech company where he spent most of his days writing code, but the sounds of motorcycles passing by on the street below often triggered intense flashbacks, causing him to feel as if he were back in a war zone. This auditory trigger had become so potent that even the smell of diesel fuel from delivery trucks nearby could transport him to the battlefield. Thompson’s life was now punctuated by these triggers, and they influenced how he navigated his world. He found himself avoiding going out, reading the news, watching TV, or engaging in any form of exercise, as each activity seemed to amplify his fear and vulnerability. His aversion to being naked had also intensified; even a quick shower made him feel exposed and unsafe, further limiting his daily activities. The memories of his combat experiences were vivid and intrusive. Whenever he heard sounds reminiscent of the battlefield, such as motorcycle noise, he would hear in his head the cacophony of gunfire and explosions from that frightening event. These auditory recollections played over and over like a film loop in his mind, making it impossible for him to escape them. The nonverbal aspects of these memories were equally haunting; he could not put the events into words, leaving him feeling isolated and unable to process what had happened. Thompson’s avoidance behaviors emerged as coping mechanisms to deal with these overwhelming triggers and memories. He felt that by avoiding places and activities that might trigger his flashbacks, he was protecting himself from further trauma. However, this strategy only served to isolate him more deeply within his own home, where he also felt on guard. His alertness at home had grown over time; even inside his own safe space, he could not shake the feeling of constant danger. The threat of harm seemed omnipresent in Thompson’s daily life. He avoided unfamiliar places because he believed that he couldn’t assess their safety adequately, and strangers approaching him were perceived as potential threats. This heightened sense of vulnerability was further reinforced by the recurring memories of combat sounds, which only intensified his need to avoid situations where such triggers could occur. Thompson’s wife noticed changes in his behavior over time. He had become increasingly withdrawn and anxious, avoiding social gatherings and even small talk at work. His avoidance behaviors extended to his professional life as well; he would often cancel meetings that required him to leave the office or interact with unfamiliar colleagues. The cycle of triggers, memories, threat perceptions, and maladaptive strategies became self-reinforcing over months. Thompson’s avoidance behaviors led to further isolation, which in turn exacerbated his sense of vulnerability and triggered more intrusive memories. The memories themselves fueled his anxiety and reinforced his need for constant vigilance. Thompson finally sought help when he realized that his condition was affecting not just himself but also his relationship with his wife. He was certain that the only way to reclaim his life was by addressing these overwhelming triggers and memories. His greatest fear was remaining trapped in a perpetual state of hypervigilance, while his greatest hope lay in finding a way to break this cycle and regain control over his daily life. Thompson’s story is one of resilience amidst trauma, where the weight of past experiences continues to shape his present reality. The intertwined connections between triggers, memories, threat perceptions, and maladaptive strategies form a complex web that he must navigate with professional support.
